briefing.summary: Dive on the summit of Kama'ehuakanaloa, the youngest volcano in the Hawaiian chain, then scan the low-temperature, iron-rich hydrothermal vents inside Pele's Pit -- the crater left by the volcano's 1996 summit collapse. Optional objectives trace the south rift zone.
facts: Renamed from Lo'ihi to Kama'ehuakanaloa in July 2021 by the Hawai'i Board on Geographic Names, restoring a name drawn from Hawaiian mele recorded decades before the 1955 descriptive name.
The summit lies roughly 975-1,000 m below sea level. Future emergence depends on eruption rates; USGS gives a speculative estimate of as much as 200,000 years.
More than 4,000 earthquakes were recorded between 16 July and 9 August 1996. Summit collapse formed Pele's Pit, about 600 m wide, with its floor about 300 m below the previous surface.
Vent fluids here are low in sulfide and rich in dissolved iron, feeding iron-oxidizing microbial mats instead of the black-smoker chimneys found at sulfide-rich vent fields.
hazards: This is an active volcano: seismic swarms and eruptions have reshaped the summit before (1996) and could again.
Research cruises measured warm diffuse fluids at Hiolo, with mean temperatures around 40-47 degC. Keep clear of active orifices.
Steep local relief around Pele's Pit and the south rift; watch altitude near the vent sites.

objectives.title: Survey Hiolo North
objectives.hint: Head southwest of the summit into Pele's Pit, near 1,300 m.

objectives.title: Survey Hiolo South
objectives.hint: Look south of the summit inside Pele's Pit, around 1,275 m.

objectives.title: Trace the south rift
objectives.hint: Follow the deepening volcanic slope south from the summit, around 1,280 m here.
